chapters.title: Chapter 3: Debt Funds, Bonds and Gold

lessons.title: Debt Mutual Funds After April 2023: Why Gains Are Taxed at Your Slab Rate

body.text: For debt funds bought on or after 1 April 2023, how long you hold no longer matters for tax. Every rupee of gain is added to your income and taxed at your slab rate, just like fixed deposit interest, except you pay only when you redeem.

children.text: Ashwin, a 36-year-old IT lead in Pune in the 30% slab, put his annual bonus into a corporate bond fund in June 2024. A colleague had told him that holding for three years would give "long-term gains with indexation". In September 2026 he redeemed with a ₹60,000 gain and discovered he owed ₹18,720 including cess, exactly as if it were FD interest. His colleague's advice had been out of date for more than a year before he even invested.

events.title: The old debt fund advantage
events.description: Units held for more than 36 months gave long-term gains taxed at 20% with indexation, often far less than FD tax for investors in higher slabs.

events.title: Deemed short-term rule arrives
events.description: Units of funds with not more than 35% in domestic equity, bought on or after this date, became short-term regardless of holding period, taxed at slab rate, with no indexation.

events.title: Older units: 24 months and 12.5%
events.description: Debt fund units bought before 1 April 2023 became long-term after 24 months, taxed at 12.5% without indexation.

events.title: Specified mutual fund redefined
events.description: The deemed short-term rule now applies to funds with more than 65% in debt and money market instruments, and to funds of funds putting 65% or more into such funds.

events.title: Section 76 of the Income-tax Act, 2025
events.description: The rule continues unchanged under section 76 of the new Act (section 50AA of the 1961 Act).

markDefs.definition: Under section 76 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 50AA of the 1961 Act), a mutual fund investing more than 65% of its total proceeds in debt and money market instruments, or a fund of funds investing 65% or more in such funds. Gains on units bought on or after 1 April 2023 are always short-term.

children.text: . If a fund is a specified mutual fund and you bought the units on or after 1 April 2023, the gain is deemed short-term under section 76 of the 2025 Act (section 50AA of the 1961 Act), whether you hold for six days or six years.

body.caption: Which funds are specified mutual funds? (units bought on or after 1 April 2023)

cells: Ultra short, short duration, corporate bond and banking and PSU funds
Gilt funds and target maturity index funds
Debt ETFs such as Bharat Bond ETF
Funds with more than 35% but not more than 65% in debt
24-month clock; 12.5% if long-term, slab rate if short-term
Arbitrage and equity savings funds (at least 65% in equity including hedged positions)

body.title: Which One Escapes the Slab Rate Rule?
body.question: Each fund below was bought in May 2025 and is redeemed in October 2027. Which gain is NOT automatically short-term?
options: Bharat Bond ETF units bought on NSE
A multi-asset fund holding about 40% debt, 35% Indian equity and 25% gold
body.explanation: The liquid fund, gilt fund and Bharat Bond ETF all hold more than 65% in debt, so they are specified mutual funds and their gains are always short-term. The multi-asset fund has only about 40% in debt and less than 65% in Indian equity, so it is neither a specified fund nor equity-oriented. Held for more than 24 months, its gain is long-term at 12.5%.

children.text: If you have held a debt fund for years, your folio may contain units from both sides of 1 April 2023. FIFO still applies, but each lot is taxed under its own rule. By now, every unit bought before 1 April 2023 has been held for more than 24 months, so those lots are all long-term.

body.label: What a Post-April 2023 Debt Fund Gain Never Gets
body.value: No LTCG. No indexation. No exemption.
body.context: Gains on specified mutual fund units bought on or after 1 April 2023 are always short-term, added to your total income and taxed at slab rates.

body.title: Ashwin's Tax Bill
body.prompt: Ashwin's corporate bond fund gain is ₹60,000. He bought the units in June 2024 and is in the 30% slab. Ignoring surcharge, what is his total tax on this gain including 4% cess, in rupees?
body.explanation: The units were bought after 1 April 2023, so the gain is short-term regardless of holding period. Tax = ₹60,000 × 30% = ₹18,000. Cess = 4% of ₹18,000 = ₹720. Total = ₹18,720.

body.title: The Lost Benefit
body.textWithBlank: Before April 2023, debt fund investors holding for more than three years could adjust their purchase cost for inflation using ___, which the new rules no longer allow.
body.explanation: Indexation raised the purchase cost using the cost inflation index, which shrank the taxable gain. It is not available on specified mutual fund units bought from 1 April 2023, and since 23 July 2024 it is not available on older debt fund units either.

children.text: So Are Debt Funds Now the Same as FDs?

Not quite. The tax rate is now the same, but timing is different. FD interest is taxed every year as it accrues, and banks deduct TDS once interest crosses the threshold. A debt fund is taxed only when you redeem, and there is no TDS on redemptions for resident investors. Compare ₹5,00,000 for three years at 7% for someone in the 30% slab.

body.title: Tax Paid Each Year on ₹5,00,000 at 7% (30% Slab, Cess Ignored)

children.text: Total tax is the same ₹33,756 in both cases, assuming identical 7% returns and annual compounding. But the FD investor pays ₹10,500 in year one and ₹11,235 in year two, while the debt fund investor keeps that money invested until redemption. Over longer periods, or if you move to a lower slab by the time you redeem, the deferral matters more.

body.text: Three advantages debt funds still keep over FDs: tax is deferred until redemption, no TDS is deducted for resident investors, and a loss on a debt fund is a capital loss that can be set off against capital gains, whereas FD interest can never create a loss.

body.text: There is a hidden upside for lower-income investors. Because debt fund gains on post-April 2023 units are taxed at slab rates rather than a special rate, they are eligible for the new-regime rebate. Equity gains taxed under sections 196 and 198 are not, as Chapter 2 showed.

body.title: Kamala's Retirement Income
body.scenario: Kamala, 64, a retired school principal in Coimbatore, is in the new tax regime. Her pension is ₹6,00,000 a year and she gets the ₹75,000 standard deduction on it. In tax year 2026-27 she redeems a banking and PSU debt fund bought in 2024, making a ₹2,00,000 gain. She has no other income.
body.prompt: How much tax does Kamala pay on her debt fund gain?
body.modelAnswer: Nothing. Her taxable income is ₹6,00,000 − ₹75,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹7,25,000. The debt fund gain is short-term and taxed at slab rates, so it is simply part of her normal income. Slab tax on ₹7,25,000 is ₹16,250, and since her total income is within ₹12 lakh, the rebate wipes that out entirely. For retirees and others in low or nil tax brackets, the post-2023 rule costs little or nothing.

body.title: Deep Dive: Funds Between 35% and 65% Debt

children.text: Funds that hold more than 35% but not more than 65% in debt fall into a middle category. They are not specified mutual funds, and unless they hold more than 65% in Indian listed equity, they are not equity-oriented either. That puts them on the 24-month clock: gains are taxed at slab rate if held for 24 months or less, and at 12.5% without indexation if held longer.

Several fund houses have launched multi-asset funds and income-plus-arbitrage funds of funds designed to sit in this band. For an investor in the 30% slab who can hold for more than two years, the difference between 30% and 12.5% is large.

content.text: A fund's tax classification depends on its actual portfolio and mandate, and can change if the mandate changes. Check the scheme information document and the fund house's stated tax treatment before investing, rather than relying on the category name alone.

cards.definition: More than 65% in debt and money market instruments, or a fund of funds with 65% or more in such funds. Section 76, 2025 Act (old 50AA).
Gains on specified fund units bought from 1 April 2023 are short-term whatever the holding period.
Long-term after 24 months, taxed at 12.5% without indexation under section 197.
Inflation adjustment of cost using the cost inflation index. No longer available on debt funds.
Debt fund gains are taxed only on redemption, unlike FD interest taxed yearly.
More than 35% but not more than 65% in debt. 24-month clock, 12.5% if long-term.

body.title: Review Your Debt Fund Holdings
steps: Download your CAS and list every debt, liquid, gilt and hybrid fund you hold
Split each folio into lots bought before 1 April 2023 and lots bought on or after that date
Check each fund's debt allocation in its scheme information document to confirm whether it is a specified mutual fund
For pre-April 2023 lots, remember gains are long-term at 12.5%
For post-April 2023 lots, estimate tax at your slab rate before redeeming
If your income will be lower in a future year, such as after retirement, consider timing redemptions for that year

points: Specified mutual fund units bought on or after 1 April 2023 are always short-term and taxed at your slab rate
From 1 April 2025, a specified mutual fund means more than 65% in debt and money market instruments
Units bought before 1 April 2023 are now long-term after 24 months and taxed at 12.5% without indexation
Debt funds still beat FDs on timing: tax only on redemption and no TDS for residents
Because these gains are taxed at slab rates, they qualify for the new-regime rebate for incomes within ₹12 lakh
Funds with more than 35% but not more than 65% in debt follow the 24-month clock and 12.5% long-term rate
